content:
I originally used the iPhone 18 Pro to shoot a series of portrait photos to test its larger aperture. The original plan was to wait until dark to see if capturing more light would shorten the exposure time in Night mode.

I postponed that test, however, because something more interesting happened: a cruise ship passed through Tower Bridge in a very rare occurrence. This was the perfect opportunity to test the new phone's night-time video capabilities…

Over the years, the iPhone has evolved into a remarkably capable camera, but there has always been a noticeable gap in quality between daytime and nighttime performance, whether shooting photos or video.

Apple has put in considerable effort in this area over the years, and the results are evident. Given how small the sensor is, the iPhone's current low-light photography capability is already quite astonishing. The addition of Night mode portraits in 2020 has helped as well.

Computational photography is key to much of the iPhone's night-shooting prowess overall. Although we think we are taking a single shot, the phone is actually capturing a burst of images behind the scenes and merging frames of different exposures into one composite image.

Video, however, is a far greater challenge. When shooting at least 24 frames per second and capturing mostly moving images, it is very difficult for the phone to capture multiple exposures within a single frame and merge them. Precisely because of this, the quality of night-time video inevitably lags far behind that of night-time photos.

Apple has indeed been pushing forward in this area, and night-time video performance improves with each generation. In addition to benefiting from Apple's annual improvements to video processing, the iPhone 18 Pro also features a larger aperture that lets in more light. Although the increase is less than one stop, every extra photon matters when it comes to video.

The full normal-speed recording runs for just over nine minutes, and I didn't want to rely solely on the phone's excellent video stabilisation for that long, so I held a mini tripod steady on top of a railing. I sped the footage up to 10x and compressed it to 96 seconds, but kept a few normal-speed segments so viewers can savour the extremely delicate operation of the tugboat.

So what was the result? Not perfect, but certainly another step forward in quality. Of course, pixel-peepers like me will say some fine detail looks a bit soft up close, but honestly, does it matter? The average viewer watching this kind of footage would just take pleasure in the moment and have no quibbles about the quality. When I look back at low-light video recordings from a few generations ago, the difference is really… night and day.

So yes, night-time video performance has yet to reach the ideal level I imagine, yet every generation improves, and this one is no exception. In fact, even in highly challenging conditions like these, we have already easily reached the point of being 'more than good enough for most people to enjoy'.
